name: Ireland (since 1922)
summary: Most of Ireland became independent from the UK as the Irish Free State in 1922 and a republic in 1949; Northern Ireland remained in the UK.

knownFor.label: Celtic Tiger
knownFor.note: Fast economic growth from the mid-1990s.

knownFor.label: Easter Rising
knownFor.note: The 1916 rebellion that led to independence.

location.value: Most of the island of Ireland; about 70,000 km².

terrain.value: Rugged cliffs, hills and mountains in the west; central lowlands with bogland and lakes. The highest point is Carrauntoohil.

climate.value: A temperate oceanic climate shaped by the Atlantic and the Gulf Stream; temperatures usually range from about −5 °C in winter to 26 °C in summer, and the southwest is wettest.

resources.value: Zinc and lead, gypsum, and offshore gas (Kinsale Head, Corrib); farming uses about 64% of the land.

disasters.value: The Great Famine (1845–1849), before independence, killed about one million people and drove 1.5 million to emigrate.

urbanisation.value: Dublin, the capital and largest city, has over 1.5 million people.

disease.value: Every resident is entitled to public health care, funded by general taxation; private providers also operate.

migration.value: Emigration kept the population falling until the 1960s; immigration has since grown, with 631,785 non-Irish nationals in 2022.

economicBase.value: Foreign multinationals drive the economy, making Ireland one of the world's largest exporters of pharmaceuticals, medical devices and software.

tradeRoutes.value: A member of the European Communities (now EU) since 1973; the EU takes 57.9% of exports.

wealth.value: Among the top five countries for GDP and GNI per capita, though GDP is inflated by multinational income that often flows out of Ireland.

moneyAndTax.value: Adopted the euro in 2002; foreign multinationals pay 80% of corporate taxes.

inequality.value: Income gaps after taxes and benefits are close to the EU average; high rents and house prices are the biggest pressure on young people.

governmentType.value: A parliamentary republic: the Taoiseach (prime minister) leads the government; the elected President is head of state with limited powers.

keyRulers.value: Michael Collins led the pro-treaty side and Éamon de Valera the anti-treaty side in 1922.

succession.value: Governments are formed after elections to the Dáil, using proportional representation with a single transferable vote; coalitions are common.

institutions.value: The Oireachtas (Dáil and Seanad), the President, a Supreme Court that can rule on whether bills are constitutional, and a written constitution adopted in 1937.

stability.value: A civil war (1922–1923) followed the treaty with Britain; in 2024 Ireland was ranked the second most peaceful country in the world.

eliteConflict.value: No single party has governed alone since 1989; the current coalition is Fianna Fáil, Fine Gael and independents, with Sinn Féin in opposition.

armyAndTech.value: Small but well-equipped Defence Forces of almost 10,000 full-time personnel, serving in UN peacekeeping since 1960, including in Cyprus, Lebanon and Bosnia.

majorWars.value: The War of Independence (ended by a truce in July 1921), then the Civil War (1922–1923); neutral in the Second World War, which it called "The Emergency".

territoryChange.value: The state covers 26 of Ireland's 32 counties; Northern Ireland stayed in the UK, and the 1998 Good Friday Agreement removed the constitutional claim to it.

alliancesRivals.value: Militarily neutral and not in NATO; joined the European Communities in 1973.

inventions.value: Irish-born scientists include Robert Boyle and William Thomson (Lord Kelvin), from before independence; modern Ireland is a hub for software and medical devices.

scienceEducation.value: Around 63% of adults aged 25–34 have a higher education qualification (2023), among the highest shares in the EU.

openness.value: An open economy that ranks first for "high-value" foreign investment; foreign multinationals employ a quarter of the private-sector workforce.

communicationTransport.value: Main airports at Dublin, Shannon and Cork; Dublin has DART trains, Luas trams and buses.

religion.value: Mostly Catholic (69.1% in 2022, down from 84.2% in 2011); voters approved same-sex marriage in 2015 and abortion was legalised in 2018.

languageWriting.value: Irish is the national and first official language, but English dominates; Irish is a community language only in the Gaeltacht.

artsArchitecture.value: World-famous writers (Joyce, Yeats, Beckett, Heaney) and Georgian townhouses, especially in Dublin.

socialStructure.value: Irish people combine Gaelic, Norse, Anglo-Norman, French and British ancestry; 631,785 non-Irish nationals lived there in 2022.

sharedIdentity.value: Gaelic football and hurling are the traditional sports; Irish culture shares features with the Anglosphere, Catholic Europe and other Celtic regions.

dailyLife.value: Popular dishes include stew, boxty, colcannon and bacon and cabbage, plus the full Irish breakfast.

neighbours.value: Its only land border is with Northern Ireland (UK); the Irish Sea lies to the east.

ideasReligions.value: The Irish diaspora, one of the world's largest, has spread Irish culture worldwide.

colonisation.value: Influenced by the Anglo-Norman invasion (12th century) and British conquest from the 16th century; part of the United Kingdom from 1801 to 1922.

riseSignals.value: Easter Rising (1916), the War of Independence and the Anglo-Irish Treaty led to the Irish Free State in 1922 and a republic in 1949.

peakPeriod.value: The "Celtic Tiger" boom (1995–2007), when Ireland became one of the world's fastest-growing economies.

declineSignals.value: The property bubble burst and banking crisis led to an €85 billion EU–IMF assistance programme and net emigration of 120,100 people (2008–2013).

overallCertainty.value: Well documented by official statistics and many histories; figures on company profits distort GDP, so other income measures are used.
